_comment: The share-pack gate's HOLD LIST -- the GENERIC STARTER, and the one that ships. Read by
Test-SharePackClean.ps1 check 4 and by Build-SharePack.ps1 when hold-classes.json is not present
beside it.
WHAT A HOLD LIST IS FOR, and why it is not the redaction check. The redaction check reads file
CONTENTS and answers 'does this text carry an identifier'. This list answers a different
question -- 'may this asset leave at all' -- and it is a question about PATHS, because the
assets that answer 'no' are frequently clean. An accumulated permission corpus is real paths and
real command history and not one organisation name; a host-teardown script is process kills
tailored to one machine; an archive's whole problem is that no text check in the pack can read
inside it. None of those would ever be caught by reading their bytes for identifiers, and the
one class here that IS about a name is about a name in the PATH, which a content scan never
sees.
THIS FILE EXISTS BECAUSE THE POPULATED TABLE CANNOT SHIP, and the argument is the redaction
table's argument arriving one check later. A populated hold list is a captioned inventory of
exactly the assets an organisation decided to withhold -- which is a map of what it has -- and a
path-shaped class has nowhere to put a name except the pattern and the worked example. So the
populated table is held back (by a class in itself: see the last two entries below, which are
the two class tables), and this one ships in its place.
NOTHING BELOW IS REAL. orgname, tenant-bundle, domain-a, host-teardown.ps1 -- every specific
name here is fictional and none of it will match anything in your tree. That is the shape
working as intended: what ships is the SCHEMA and the reasoning, and the vocabulary is yours to
write. Four of the classes are NOT fictional and are worth keeping as they stand, because they
are properties of the tooling rather than of an organisation: the two settings files, the
generated memory index, the archive class and the compiled-residue class.
TO STAND THE GATE UP: copy this file to hold-classes.json beside it, replace the fictional
patterns with your own withheld assets, and leave the last two entries alone -- they are what
keeps your populated tables out of what YOU distribute, for exactly the reason this paragraph
describes. The gate and the builder both prefer hold-classes.json and fall back to this file,
and both name the table they loaded in their report, so until you write one every run says out
loud that it was holding back placeholder paths.
AND THAT NOTE IS NOT A FORMALITY. A run against this table withholds nothing you own. It
exercises the plumbing -- the file loads, the classes parse, every example still matches its own
pattern, every counter-example still does not, the walk applies them, the report prints -- and it
certifies nothing whatever about your withheld assets. Do not read a green HoldList line under
these patterns as evidence that nothing sensitive shipped.
REQUIRED KEYS -- the same four the redaction table requires, deliberately, so there is one shape
to learn:
name             Appears verbatim in every finding. Name the asset, not the regex.
pattern          A .NET regex, matched against the PACK-RELATIVE path with forward slashes.
CASE-SENSITIVE unless you write (?i).
example          A path the pattern MUST match, checked on EVERY run rather than only in a
self-test. A pattern that has stopped matching withholds nothing, reports
nothing, and looks exactly like a pack with nothing to withhold. This one key
is what stands between a broken class and a gate that silently permits
everything.
counter_example  Optional, and worth writing wherever the class runs close to something the
pack legitimately ships: the near-miss, asserted NOT to match. A class too
broad withholds a file the recipient needed, which is how people learn to
route around the gate.
reason           Required. Why this must not leave.
THE GATE AND THE BUILDER BOTH THROW rather than passing if neither this file nor
hold-classes.json is present, or if the table they do load holds no classes. A hold list that
failed to load permits everything, and it must never report PASS.

classes.name: accumulated permission corpus
classes.reason: The rule corpus a real host accumulates: real paths, real hostnames, real command history. Its aggregate statistics are the shareable part and the file is not. Keep this class as it stands -- the filename is the tool's, not yours.

classes.name: live host settings
classes.reason: A live settings file carries endpoints, and frequently a credential, under its server configuration. Ship the floor-only template instead. The counter-example is that template, one word away from the held name -- which is the reason this pattern is anchored on the full filename.

classes.name: generated memory index
classes.reason: A generated index is a table of contents for whatever the author has been working on. The toolkit that generates one ships; a generated one does not.

classes.name: pinned internal policy source
classes.reason: Fictional as written -- rename these to whatever your compliance layer pins. The genre is a file holding document-host identifiers, internal contacts and pinned control text; ship the schema and the empty headings, never the data.

classes.name: host-specific automation
classes.reason: Fictional names. The genre is a script that kills processes or force-merges branches on one specific machine: correct there, destructive anywhere else, and impossible for a recipient to review against a host they cannot see.

classes.name: front door to withheld machinery
classes.reason: Fictional names. Whatever you withhold above, withhold its documented entry point too: shipping the front door to something deliberately absent is worse than shipping neither, because it reads as a defect in the pack rather than as a decision.

classes.name: domain deliverable
classes.reason: Fictional directory names. The genre is subject-matter work that happens to live in the same tree as the practice toolkits: out of scope for a coding-practice pack, and usually confidential besides. The counter-example is a teaching example that must keep shipping.

classes.name: tenant distribution route
classes.reason: Fictional. The genre is a directory whose layout is dictated by one deployment target: it names the deployment, and everything under it reaches a place the recipient cannot.

classes.name: name carrying the organisation
classes.reason: Replace 'orgname' with your own prefix. Assets that ship renamed off an organisation prefix need a class that catches the un-renamed form, and a redaction check reads file CONTENTS and would never see a name that only exists in the path.

classes.name: opaque archive
classes.reason: No text check in a pack like this can read inside an archive, so shipping one exempts its contents from every gate at once. Ship the unpacked files. Keep this class as it stands.

classes.name: build residue
classes.reason: Compiled residue: unreadable by every text check, and useless to a recipient. The builder's non-content exclusion normally drops it before this list is consulted, so a hit here means it arrived by some other route. Keep this class as it stands.

classes.name: real redaction class table
classes.reason: KEEP THIS CLASS. Once you write your own redaction-classes.json it becomes a captioned list of every identifier you know about, which is why it was put in a data file in the first place -- so that it could be withheld. The .example table beside it is the generic starter and MUST keep shipping; the two names are one word apart and carry opposite verdicts, which is what the counter-example holds.

classes.name: real hold class table
classes.reason: KEEP THIS CLASS. Once you write your own hold-classes.json it becomes a captioned inventory of the assets you decided to withhold, which is a map of what you have. It is also the one asset on the list whose absence nobody would notice, so a hold list that does not hold itself back is a hold list that eventually ships.
